name: No em dashes

source.quote: Em dash (—). Don't use it. Readers now associate the em dash with machine-written text, and every job it does has a clearer replacement.

message: The em dash is the strongest machine-written tell, and every job it does has a clearer replacement. A double hyphen is treated as an em dash in Markdown.
fix: For an aside, use a pair of commas or parentheses. To introduce a list, use a colon. To join two statements, use a period and two sentences.

flag: Archived projects — those older than a year — are read-only.
Archived projects -- the old ones -- are read-only.
pass: Archived projects, those older than a year, are read-only.
Sync runs every 15 minutes (or right away, if you select Sync now).

name: En dash used as a dash

source.quote: En dash (–). Use it for number and date ranges, with no spaces: 2016–2026. In a UI time range, spaces are fine.

message: A spaced en dash is doing an em dash's job. The en dash is for ranges only.
fix: Replace it the way you would an em dash: commas, parentheses, a colon, or a period.

flag: Archived projects – those older than a year – are read-only.

name: No semicolons

source.quote: Don't use them. Readers rarely see semicolons outside formal writing, and a sentence that needs one is usually two sentences or a list.

message: A sentence that needs a semicolon is usually two sentences or a list.
fix: Split the sentence, or turn the series into a list.

flag: The sync finished; three files were skipped.
pass: The sync finished. Three files were skipped.

name: No exclamation points

source.section: Punctuation > Exclamation points and question marks
source.quote: Don't use exclamation points in UI or documentation.

message: An exclamation point reads as shouting in an error and as gushing in a success message.
fix: End the sentence with a period.

flag: Your changes have been successfully saved to the system!

name: Straight quotation marks

source.quote: Use straight quotation marks (" "), not curly ones. They render the same in every font, browser, and code editor.

message: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes usually come from a word processor. They don't render the same everywhere, and they break copied values.
fix: Replace with the straight character: " or '.

name: Periods and commas go inside the closing quotation mark

source.quote: Put periods and commas inside the closing quotation mark. Exception: when the quoted text is a literal value, such as a search term or a file name, put the punctuation outside.

message: US convention puts the period or comma inside the closing quotation mark. A literal value such as a search term or file name is the exception (No projects match "sales".), so this check only suggests.
fix: Move the period or comma inside the quotation mark, unless the quoted text is a literal value.

flag: If you see "Sync paused", check your connection.
pass: If you see "Sync paused," check your connection.

name: One space after a period

source.quote: Use one space after a period.

message: Two spaces after a period is a typewriter habit that shows up as uneven gaps.
fix: Use one space.

flag: Project saved.  Open it to continue.
pass: Project saved. Open it to continue.

name: Use and, not an ampersand

source.quote: Use and. Keep an ampersand only when it's part of a name or a UI label.

message: An ampersand reads as a symbol, not a word, and translation tools often leave it alone.
fix: Write "and", unless the ampersand is part of a name or an existing UI label.

pass: Projects and tasks sync every hour.

name: Don't use a slash for or

source.quote: Don't use a slash in place of or. "Select a project/task" becomes "Select a project or a task."

message: A slash asks the reader to guess whether you mean "and", "or", or both. Fixed pairs such as on/off and read/write are fine.
fix: Write "or" (or "and"). "And/or" almost always means "or".

flag: Add a member and/or a team.
pass: Select a project or a task to open.

name: Don't nest parentheses

source.quote: Don't nest them.

message: Nested parentheses mean the sentence is carrying two asides. One is already one too many.
fix: Move one aside into its own sentence, or drop it.

flag: Sync runs every hour (or sooner (if you select Sync now)).
pass: Sync runs every hour (or sooner, if you select Sync now).

name: No hyphen after an -ly adverb

source.quote: Don't hyphenate after an adverb ending in -ly: a newly created project.

message: An adverb ending in -ly already attaches to the next word, so the hyphen is redundant.
fix: Remove the hyphen: "a newly created project".

pass: A newly created project is empty.

name: Spell out both parts of a compound

source.quote: Spell out both parts instead of suspending a compound. Write first-level and second-level headings, not first- and second-level headings.

message: A suspended hyphen asks the reader to reassemble the word.
fix: Repeat the second part: "first-level and second-level headings".

name: Most prefixes take no hyphen

source.quote: Most prefixes take no hyphen: autoscale, preview, rerun, nonzero, multifactor. Hyphenate when the word would be misread without one (re-create, re-sort), or when the next character is a capital letter or a numeral.

message: Most prefixes join the word with no hyphen. The hyphen stays only when the word would be misread or the next character is a capital or a numeral.
fix: Close the word: "rerun", "nonzero", "multifactor". Use the hyphen only in cases such as "re-create" and "non-English".

name: No period or ellipsis at the end of a heading

source.quote: No period at the end. A question mark is fine when the heading asks the reader's question.

message: Headings and labels take no end punctuation other than a question mark.
fix: Remove the period or ellipsis.

pass: ## What is a service level objective?

name: Never end a heading with a colon

source.quote: Never end a heading or a UI label with a colon.

message: A heading introduces the section by itself. The colon adds nothing.
fix: Remove the colon.

name: Headings use sentence case

source.quote: Use sentence case for headings, titles, labels, buttons, menu items, tooltips, column headers, and list items. Capitalize the first word and proper nouns.

message: This heading looks like title case: two or more words after the first are capitalized. Proper nouns and acronyms stay capitalized, so check that the capitals are names.
fix: Capitalize only the first word, proper nouns, and the first word after a colon.

name: Capitalize the first word after a colon in a heading

source.quote: In a heading or title, also capitalize the first word after a colon. Version 4.2: What changed for admins

message: In a heading, the word after a colon starts a new clause and takes a capital.
fix: Capitalize the word after the colon.

name: No ampersands or plus signs in headings

source.quote: Avoid ampersands and plus signs.

message: Symbols in a heading read as abbreviations and don't translate.
fix: Write "and".

name: Don't introduce an acronym in a heading

source.quote: Don't introduce an acronym in a heading.

message: The expansion belongs in the text that follows, where the reader can see it in context.
fix: Use either the spelled-out term or the acronym in the heading, and introduce the pair in the first paragraph.

name: No semicolons, commas, or conjunctions at the ends of list items

source.quote: No semicolons, commas, or conjunctions at the ends of items.

message: A list item stands on its own. Trailing punctuation or conjunctions turn the list back into a sentence.
fix: Remove the trailing semicolon, comma, or conjunction.

pass:
- Create a project
- Add members
- Set the access rule

name: Start each list item with a capital letter

source.quote: Start each item with a capital letter.

message: List items start with a capital letter, even when they're fragments. A code value or identifier that must stay lowercase is the exception, and it belongs in code style.
fix: Capitalize the first word, or put a lowercase identifier in code style.

name: Lowercase after a colon in a sentence

source.quote: After a colon in a sentence, lowercase the next word unless it's a proper noun. In a heading or title, capitalize it.

message: Inside a sentence, the word after a colon stays lowercase unless it's a proper noun. This check can't tell a name from a common word, so it only suggests.
fix: Lowercase the word after the colon unless it's a name.

flag: Each task has three dates: Created, due, and closed.
pass: Each task has three dates: created, due, and closed.
Optional: In Message, add a note.

name: Use a leading zero below one

source.quote: Decimals. Use a leading zero below one: 0.5.

message: A bare decimal point is easy to miss.
fix: Write the zero: 0.5.
